articleOfWeek.title: Discordant evidence on corticosteroids in sepsis: a meta-research study.
articleOfWeek.abstract: Despite an extensive evidence base of randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and systematic reviews (SRs), current sepsis guidelines provide only weak recommendations for corticosteroid therapy, while available SRs report conflicting mortality conclusions. We aimed to characterize the evidence landscape of SRs evaluating corticosteroids for sepsis, including their clinical scope, underlying RCT evidence bases, mortality conclusions, and to explore potential sources of discordance. Meta-research study of SRs on corticosteroids in sepsis published between 2015 and 2025. Study-pool overlap was assessed using a SR×RCT inclusion matrix, Jaccard similarity (J), and hierarchical clustering. SRs and RCTs were classified according to standardized Population, Intervention, Comparison, Outcome (PICO) profiles. We explored discordance in short-term mortality conclusions among clinically comparable SRs and potential associations with study-pool composition, target populations, and methodological characteristics. Forty-two SRs including 121 unique RCTs were identified. More than half of pairwise SR comparisons shared no RCTs, and only three pairs showed high overlap (J > 0.8). SRs addressing similar intervention and target population profiles frequently relied on different study pools. Among 38 SRs with short-term mortality meta-analyses, 15 (39%) reported benefit and 23 (61%) no evidence of effect. Discordance occurred exclusively among SRs evaluating broad, non-specific corticosteroid strategies; conclusions were consistent for hydrocortisone plus fludrocortisone (benefit) and hydrocortisone, ascorbic acid, and thiamine (no evidence of effect). SRs including adult sepsis ± shock populations more frequently reported benefit than those restricted to septic shock (62% vs 22%), although this comparison was based on only 22 SRs evaluating broad, non-specific corticosteroid strategies and estimates were imprecise. No single methodological or clinical factor consistently explained discordance. SRs addressing apparently similar clinical questions frequently synthesized different underlying evidence bases and reported discordant conclusions. When selecting SRs to inform clinical decisions and recommendations for sepsis management, clinicians and guideline developers should consider not only methodological quality and reported PICO, but also whether the included RCTs adequately represent the intended clinical question.

articles.title: Bedside ECMO Cannulation by Intensivists and Emergency Physicians.
articles.abstract: The number of centers capable of initiating extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) for critically ill patients with refractory cardiac or respiratory failure is expanding. Historically, patients were taken to the operating room or catheterization laboratory for ECMO cannulation by cardiothoracic surgeons and perfusionists. More recently, non-surgeons who have undergone specialized training are performing percutaneous ECMO cannulation and initiation of support at the bedside at some centers. This approach is attractive, in part, because of the timely initiation of ECMO and avoidance of the risk of patient deterioration during transport to a procedural area. The purpose of this article is to provide a roadmap for intensivists and emergency physicians to lead ECMO bedside procedures including veno-venous (VV), veno-arterial (VA), and hybrid veno-arteriovenous (V-AV) cannulation at ECMO-capable centers. These procedures demand cognitive and technical skills that are already foundational to critical care practice, including vascular access guided by point-of-care ultrasound and leadership during a dynamic resuscitation. A team-based approach to bedside ECMO cannulation is presented and illustrated with figures and video, including preparation, procedural execution, subsequent patient management, and programmatic considerations such as training and credentialing requirements.

articles.title: Emergency department care experiences of patients with a migration history: a systematic mixed-studies review.
articles.abstract: Migration is a global phenomenon with significant implications for healthcare systems, requiring emergency departments (EDs) to adapt to increasingly diverse populations. While the ED often serves as the primary access point to the healthcare system for patients with a migration history (PMH), their specific care experiences have remained fragmented across literature. This systematic mixed-studies review synthesizes research on the care experiences of PMH in the ED in order to identify actionable insights for making ED care more equitable. MEDLINE, EMBASE, CINAHL, and PsycINFO were systematically searched, complemented by reference screening. Eligible studies reported primary empirical data on adult PMH in general EDs. Two reviewers independently screened studies and assessed methodological quality using the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool. Study characteristics were extracted using a piloted form. Findings were synthesized using convergent qualitative synthesis with inductive thematic analysis. 37 studies from high-income countries were included. The findings can be divided into three major themes: (1) patient evaluations of ED care, (2) language as a central barrier, and (3) perceived discrimination, fairness and exclusion. Satisfaction varied and was often lower for PMH in specific domains, while moderate to high overall satisfaction frequently coexisted with unmet needs. These evaluations were shaped by patients' prior experiences and expectations. Language barriers strongly influenced patient understanding, autonomy and participation, with inconsistent and ad-hoc interpreter use contributing to communication gaps. Many PMH reported experiences of discrimination or unfair treatment linked to race, ethnicity, language, or migration status, often embedded in broader structural conditions of healthcare. Language barriers and discrimination are important factors shaping how PMH experience ED care, while satisfaction ratings may not reliably reflect the quality or equity of care. Addressing these inequities requires sustained institutional and policy-level action, including consistent access to professional interpreters, strengthened communication practices, and institutional strategies to prevent discrimination, support patient participation, and embed equity in clinical routines and policies. PROSPERO CRD42020105332.

Earlier Application of Methylene Blue in Vasoplegic, Adrenergic Vasopressor-Resistant Patients is Associated with Better Clinical Outcomes. A Retrospective Analysis of 464 Patients.
articles.abstract: Severe shock hails a dismal prognosis for patients in intensive care units. Vasoplegic patients, refractory to adrenergic catecholamines face an increased risk for in-hospital mortality. However, the optimal timing for Methylene Blue (MB) in these vasopressor-resistant patients, remains unclear. This was a retrospective, single-center study conducted in the intensive care unit (ICU) of a tertiary medical center. 464 patients were included, 183 (39%) admitted to the general ICU and 281 (61%) to the cardiothoracic ICU. All patients developed vasoplegia and were treated with MB after a median time of 11.2 hours from admission. In the aggregated cohort, earlier MB administration was associated with lower ICU mortality (30% vs. 52%, p < 0.001), lower in-hospital mortality (41% vs. 59%, p < 0.001), lower 1-year mortality (46% vs. 62%, p < 0.001), and reduced need for continuous Veno venous hemofiltration (33% vs. 53%, p < 0.001). In survival analyses of the whole cohort, earlier MB administration was associated with reduced in-hospital mortality in univariate analysis (HR = 0.64; 95% CI 0.47-0.86, p = 0.003) and remained significant after multivariable adjustment (HR = 0.69; 95% CI 0.51-0.94, p = 0.018). ICU-specific analyses attenuated the association. In this retrospective, single-center cohort, earlier administration of MB was associated with improved clinical outcomes among ICU patients treated for vasoplegia, including lower mortality and reduced need for renal replacement therapy. Prospective studies are warranted to determine whether earlier MB administration should be incorporated into treatment protocols for adrenergic vasopressor-resistant vasoplegia.

Total gastric and intragastric air volumes in immediate post-resuscitation whole-body computed tomography after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest: Association with airway management, aspiration, diaphragmatic position and initial blood gas analysis.
articles.abstract: Gastric distension (GD) may occur during cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR), but quantitative human data after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) remain limited. We quantified gastric volumes after OHCA and explored associations with prehospital airway strategy, CT-defined aspiration, diaphragmatic position, and initial blood gases. This retrospective single-center study included OHCA patients undergoing post-resuscitation whole-body computed tomography (CT) within 180 minutes of emergency department (ED) admission between January 1, 2020, and March 31, 2025. Total gastric volume (TGV) and intragastric air volume (GAV) were quantified by CT volumetry. Of 255 identified patients, 120 underwent CT within 180 minutes. Median TGV was 594 mL and correlated strongly with GAV (p < 0.001). Among patients with an advanced airway at ED arrival, neither TGV (p = 0.20) nor GAV (p = 0.24) differed significantly between the tracheal airway (TA; n = 87) and supraglottic airway (SGA; n = 28) groups. CT-defined aspiration was numerically more frequent with SGA than TA (78.6% vs. 57.5%; OR 2.7; p = 0.071), whereas neither TGV nor GAV was associated with CT-defined aspiration. Weak positive correlations were observed between initial pCO2 and both TGV (ρ = 0.16; one-tailed p = 0.037) and GAV (ρ = 0.19; one-tailed p = 0.018). Gastric volumes were high in this selected post-OHCA immediate CT (< 180 minutes) cohort. No significant differences were detected according to recorded prehospital airway strategy, and gastric volume was not associated with CT-defined aspiration. Mechanisms and clinical consequences remain uncertain and require prospective studies before preventive/ therapeutic implications can be established.

Liberation from Veno-venous Extracorporeal Life Support (VV-ECLS) for Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome (ARDS): the Liberate VV-ECLS study: an international survey.
articles.abstract: The use of veno-venous extracorporeal life support (VV-ECLS) for severe acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) has increased substantially worldwide. However, approaches to liberation from extracorporeal support remain poorly defined, with no standardized protocols or validated readiness criteria. What are the global practices for VV-ECLS liberation among Extracorporeal Life Support Organization (ELSO) centers? Where is there variability in readiness assessment, liberation strategies, and use of standardized protocols? We formulated a cross-sectional survey of 25 questions regarding liberation practices among ECLS providers. Questions focused on assessed parameters for readiness to liberate, determination of liberation success, and strategies to optimize it. Surveys were distributed electronically to 765 institutions globally registered with ELSO between July 1st and Aug 15th, 2022. Descriptive statistics were used to summarize responses. Of 765 centers contacted, 340 (44%) responded, with 209 (61%) reporting use of VV-ECLS. Most centers were adult-focused, intensivist-led programs with moderate annual volumes. Most respondents (58%) prioritized VV-ECLS liberation before liberation from mechanical ventilation. Readiness for liberation was most determined by improvement in oxygenation under lung-protective ventilation (92%) and respiratory system compliance (90%), while fewer centers used inspiratory effort indices (34%). Liberation strategies were heterogeneous, with progressive reduction of sweep gas flow being most common (40%). Liberation trial duration varied widely (median 120 minutes; mean 497 ± 635 minutes), and most centers performed one trial per day. Arterial blood gas abnormalities (90%) and clinical signs of respiratory distress were the primary indicators of liberation failure. Only 42% of centers reported using a formal liberation protocol. VV-ECLS liberation practices vary substantially across centers and are largely guided by institutional experience rather than standardized evidence. These findings highlight the need for validated physiologic predictors and protocolized strategies to optimize safe and timely liberation from VV-ECLS.

authors: and members of the Coma in Latin America (COMA LATAM) group, on behalf of the Latin American Brain Injury Consortium (LABIC) and the Curing Coma Campaign
Colombia and Costa Rica and Cuba and Dominican Republic and Ecuador and El Salvador and Guatemala and Honduras and Mexico and Panama and Paraguay and Peru and Puerto Rico and Uruguay and Venezuela
articles.abstract: To determine the point prevalence of coma across Latin American critical care units, characterize its etiology, and explore short-term outcomes. Multinational, cross-sectional point prevalence study with exploratory 14-day follow-up assessment. Three hundred ninety-two hospitals across 19 Latin American countries, including ICUs, intermediate care units, neurocritical care units, cardiovascular ICUs, and trauma ICUs. Adult patients (≥ 18 yr) meeting the Coma Epidemiology, Evaluation, and Therapy care survey (COME-TOGETHER) criteria on May 28, 2024. Patients under deep sedation or pharmacological coma induction were excluded unless the coma state preceded pharmacological intervention. None (observational study). Among 8305 critically ill patients, 1145 met coma criteria (point prevalence 13.8%), with country-specific rates ranging from 5.1% to 36.8%. Individual patient data were available for 729 patients (63.7%). Traumatic brain injury was the leading individual cause (24.8%), followed by hypoxic-anoxic brain injury (14.6%) and intracerebral hemorrhage (13.5%). When categorized by pathophysiology, vascular causes predominated (48.6%), followed by traumatic brain injury (24.8%) and other causes (26.6%). Age-stratified analysis revealed trauma predominantly affecting younger patients, while cerebrovascular causes predominated in older groups. Among patients with 14-day follow-up data (29% of cohort), mortality was 29.2%, with 67.7% of survivors recovering from coma. Only the Charlson Comorbidity Index was independently associated with implementation of life-sustaining therapy limitations (adjusted odds ratio, 1.22; 95% CI, 1.15-1.30; p < 0.001). Coma affects nearly one in seven ICU beds across Latin America, with substantial country variation and distinct age-dependent etiology patterns. The significant burden highlights the need for targeted prevention strategies and specialized neurocritical care resources throughout the region.

Atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease risk prediction in individuals with and without impaired spirometry.
articles.abstract: Cardiovascular disease risk scores likely underestimate risk in individuals with impaired spirometry (airflow obstruction and preserved ratio impaired spirometry (PRISm)). How do risk scores perform between individuals with impaired and normal spirometry, and can they be improved by adding spirometry and dyspnea? Ten-year incidence of major cardiovascular events (MACE) ie., myocardial infarction, stroke or death from coronary heart disease, from 7 US population-based cohorts was used for this analysis. The pooled cohorts' equations' (PCE) ability to predict MACE was compared between normal and impaired spirometry. Cox-models adding spirometry, dyspnea to PCE variables were evaluated for improvement in MACE prediction. Among 26523 participants, those with impaired (N=7547) compared with normal (N=18932) spirometry had a higher incidence of MACE (14% vs 7%), hazard ratio 95%CI 1.25[1.17,1.34] adjusted for PCE variables. Discrimination using area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC)95%CI of the PCE for MACE was 0.792[0.780,0.803] vs 0.740[0.724,0.755] in normal vs impaired spirometry. Discrimination of MACE improved slightly by adding to the PCE: dyspnea plus 1)impaired spirometry 0.792[0.783,0.800], 2)PRISm, mild, moderate+ airflow obstruction 0.792[0.783,0.801], 3)FEV1%predicted, FEV1/FVC splines 0.793[0.784,0.802], compared with PCE variables 0.790[0.781,0.798]. The differences in AUC[95%CI] were: 1)0.002[0.001,0.003]p=0.002, 2)0.002[0.001,0.004]p=0.002, 3)0.003[0.002,0.005]p=0.0005 respectively. Among participants with impaired spirometry, only the model that added FEV1%predicted, FEV1/FVC continuous and dyspnea to the PCE showed improvement in AUC[95%CI], 0.750[0.735,0.765] vs 0.746[0.730,0.761] for PCE variables, difference of 0.004[0.001,0.008]p=0.008. There were no differences among models in calibration, sensitivity, specificity, overall performance, and after bootstrapping 1000 samples. Performance of the PCE was better among individuals with normal vs impaired spirometry, despite the latter having an excess burden of MACE. Adding spirometry and dyspnea to PCE variables showed a small statistically significant improvement in MACE prediction, which may not be meaningful clinically, so other risk factors should be considered.

ICU Mortality Associated With Clinically Important Upper Gastrointestinal Bleeding: A Multistate Analysis.
articles.abstract: Clinically important upper gastrointestinal bleeding may increase mortality and time to discharge from the ICU. Conventional analyses ignore timing and treat bleeding as a binary event. We evaluated the association between time-dependent clinically important upper gastrointestinal bleeding and ICU mortality. A multicenter cohort study using data from an international stress ulcer prophylaxis trial. A total of 4821 invasively ventilated adult participants. None. A multistate model was specified with two transient ICU states (bleed-free and post-bleed) and four absorbing states (ICU discharge or death, each with or without bleeding). The Aalen-Johansen method was used to estimate transition and state occupancy probabilities and to describe risks of different clinical courses. Follow-up was censored at 90 days. We fit two Cox models for time to death in the ICU regressing on time-dependent bleeding history while adjusting for age, sex, baseline Acute Physiology and Chronic Health Evaluation II score, admission category (medical/surgical/trauma), vasopressor/inotrope use and renal replacement therapy on study day 1 and randomized allocation of pantoprazole or placebo; a second model also adjusted for time-dependent covariates of advanced life support (invasive mechanical ventilation, vasopressor/inotrope use, and renal replacement therapy). Clinically important upper gastrointestinal bleeding developed in 104 patients (2.2%) in the ICU. Median ICU length of stay for those who experienced bleeding was 19 days (interquartile range [IQR], 11-30 d) vs. 9 days (IQR, 5-15 d) for those who did not. Accounting for immortal time bias, the time-dependent indicator of clinically important upper gastrointestinal bleeding was associated with increased ICU mortality (hazard ratio, 1.56; 95% CI, 1.13-2.15). At any time, patients who experienced bleeding had approximately 1.6 times the hazard of ICU mortality compared with those without a history of bleeding. Clinically important upper gastrointestinal bleeding as a time-dependent event is associated with an increased risk of ICU mortality.

articles.title: Age-Related Differences in the Organ Donation Process Among Pediatric Brain-Dead Donors: A Nationwide Study in Japan.
articles.abstract: To characterize the pediatric organ donation process and age-related differences among brain-dead donors in Japan and evaluate organ-specific transplantation rates and graft survival across age groups. Nationwide retrospective cohort study. National donor records maintained by the Japan Organ Transplant Network. All pediatric (≤ 17 yr old) brain-dead organ donors in Japan between July 17, 2010, and March 31, 2024. None. A total of 100 pediatric brain-dead organ donors were included. Donors were categorized into three age groups: younger than 6 years (n = 32), 6-14 years (n = 48), and 15-17 years (n = 20). The time intervals from hospital admission to organ procurement showed marked age-dependent prolongation, with median durations of 28, 19.5, and 13.5 days, respectively (p < 0.01). Younger donors were more frequently managed in children's hospitals and pediatric departments, whereas older donors were increasingly managed in emergency and critical care settings. Organ transplantation was achieved in 99% of donors. Organ-specific transplantation rates were consistently high for the heart, liver, and kidneys across all age groups, whereas lung and pancreas transplantation rates increased with donor age. During donor management, respiratory, cardiovascular, renal, and hepatic function were generally maintained or improved until procurement. No significant age-related differences in graft survival were observed for any organ type. The pediatric organ donation process in Japan was substantially prolonged in an age-dependent manner, particularly among donors younger than 6 years. Despite prolonged donor management, transplantation rates remained high, and no significant age-related differences in graft survival were observed. These findings highlight the importance of sustained multidisciplinary and family support throughout the donation process and may provide insights for pediatric donation systems in low-volume settings.

articles.title: Propranolol administration following traumatic brain injury induces distinct neuroinflammatory gene expression profiles.
articles.journal: The journal of trauma and acute care surgery
articles.abstract: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) remains a major cause of morbidity and is frequently followed by prolonged intensive care stays with sustained physiologic stress. Beta-blockade has been investigated as an adjunct therapy for TBI given its potential to reduce sympathetic hyperactivation. The molecular mechanisms underlying neuroinflammatory signaling remain incompletely defined. We hypothesized that propranolol (BB) administration following TBI would modify neuroinflammatory transcriptional responses consistent with attenuation of maladaptive inflammatory signaling. Male Sprague-Dawley rats (n=6-8/group) were divided into 6 groups: (1) TBI7d (controlled cortical impact) followed by 7 days of daily handling, (2) TBI7d with daily propranolol administration (TBI BB7d), (3) TBI with chronic restraint stress for 7 days (TBI CRS7d), (4) TBI CRS7d with daily propranolol administration (TBI CRS BB7d), (5) CRS7d (n=7) who underwent daily stress exposure for 7 days; and (6) CRS BB7d (n=7) underwent daily stress exposure with propranolol injections for 7 days. RNA was extracted from the injured frontal lobe and analyzed using the NanoString Neuroinflammation panel. Differential gene expression was analyzed using ROSALIND. Significant differentially expressed genes (sDEGs) were defined as fold change ≥1.5 or ≤-1.5 with p<0.05. Functional pathway analysis was performed using Qiagen Ingenuity Pathway Analysis. Compared with TBI alone, TBI BB7d demonstrated 83 sDEGs, including genes associated with neuronal signaling, neurotransmitter regulation, and epigenetic modulation. Pathway analysis identified significant involvement of the IL8 signaling and FXR/RXR. In the TBI CRS7d model, propranolol treatment yielded 21 sDEGs. These genes were enriched in pathways related to cellular stress responses and inflammatory regulation. Propranolol downregulated IL6, IL8, and neuroinflammation signaling pathways. Propranolol administration following TBI, with and without stress, resulted in distinct neuroinflammatory transcriptional profiles. Propranolol was associated with alterations in multiple pathways involved in stress response, immune regulation, and neurorecovery. These findings suggest beta-blockade may modulate stress-related neuroinflammatory signaling following TBI.

articles.title: High-Flow Nasal Cannula Versus Conventional Oxygen Therapy in Adults With De Novo Acute Hypoxemic Respiratory Failure: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis With Trial Sequential Analysis.
articles.abstract: To evaluate the efficacy of high-flow nasal cannula (HFNC) compared with conventional oxygen therapy (COT) in adults with de novo acute hypoxemic respiratory failure (AHRF) using a meta-analysis with trial sequential analysis (TSA). MEDLINE, Embase, and the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials were searched from database inception to April 7, 2026. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing HFNC with COT in adults with de novo AHRF. Two investigators independently performed study selection, data extraction, risk-of-bias assessment, and certainty assessment, with discrepancies resolved through discussion. A total of 13 RCTs involving 4294 patients were included in the analysis. Compared with COT, HFNC was associated with a lower risk of intubation (Risk ratio [RR], 0.88; 95% CI, 0.78-0.99; low certainty), but not mortality (RR, 0.96; 95% CI, 0.83-1.10; moderate certainty). TSA indicated that the cumulative evidence was insufficient to establish a conclusive effect for either outcome. Although HFNC was associated with a statistically significant reduction in hospital length of stay (mean difference, -0.84 d; 95% CI, -1.26 to -0.43; low certainty), the clinical importance of this reduction remains uncertain. No significant differences were observed in escalation of therapy (RR, 0.87; 95% CI, 0.75-1.01; very low certainty), ICU admission (RR, 0.84; 95% CI, 0.50-1.39; very low certainty), or ICU length of stay (mean difference, -0.10 d; 95% CI, -0.82 to 0.61; very low certainty). In adults with de novo AHRF, HFNC may reduce the need for endotracheal intubation but probably does not improve survival compared with COT.

articles.title: The Radiographic Lung Edema Score in Pediatric Acute Respiratory Failure: Associations With Systemic Inflammatory Biomarkers and Multiple Organ Dysfunction.
articles.abstract: Although chest radiographs (CXR) are among the most used imaging modalities in critically ill patients, their interpretation and clinical significance remain incompletely leveraged. The Radiographic Lung Edema (RALE) score is a prognostic bedside tool widely applied in adults to quantify lung edema on CXR. However, this score has been infrequently studied in children, and its potential to reflect broader aspects of critical illness pathophysiology beyond the lungs is unknown. We sought to determine the reproducibility of the RALE score, and whether higher RALE scores were associated with circulating inflammatory and endothelial biomarkers, multi-organ dysfunction, and worse clinical outcomes in pediatric acute respiratory failure (ARF). Retrospective cohort study. Multicenter PICUs. Critically ill children (2 wk to 17 yr old) receiving invasive mechanical ventilation (IMV) for ARF, enrolled in the CAF-PINT (Coagulation and Fibrinolysis in Pediatric Insulin Titration) study (2012-2016). None. A baseline RALE score was calculated for each patient from a single CXR obtained within 72 hours of IMV initiation. Among 212 patients, RALE scores demonstrated good inter-rater reliability (intra-class coefficient 0.85; 95% CI, 0.82-0.87). After adjustment for ARF etiology and illness severity, higher RALE scores were associated with fewer 28-day ventilator-free days (sub-distribution hazard ratio per 1-sd increase, 0.81; 95% CI, 0.69-0.95). Structural equation modeling demonstrated that this association was mediated through both pulmonary dysfunction, measured by the oxygenation index (β -0.14; 95% bootstrapped CI, -0.22 to -0.06), and extrapulmonary organ dysfunction, measured by the Pediatric Logistic Organ Dysfunction score (β -0.05; 95% bootstrapped CI, -0.10 to -0.002). Similar associations were observed for 28-day PICU-free days. Finally, penalized regression selected soluble triggering receptor expressed on myeloid cells-1, intercellular adhesion molecule-1, and tumor necrosis factor receptor-1 as biomarkers associated with higher RALE scores. We provide evidence that the RALE score is not solely a lung injury marker but also reflects broader systemic pathophysiology. These findings have important implications for the interpretation and clinical application of this bedside tool in pediatric ARF.

articles.title: Religion and Religiosity in End-of-Life Decisions in Neurocritical Care.
articles.abstract: End-of-life decisions are shaped by diverse biographical, social, and cultural factors. Few studies have systematically examined the impact of religion on end-of-life decisions, and even less data are available on religiosity (i.e., strength of religious faith). The Religion and religiosity in End-of-life deCisiOns in neuroCritIcaL carE (RECONCILE) study aimed to investigate whether religiosity, rather than religion, plays a decisive role in shaping end-of-life decisions. Prospective observational study. The study was conducted between 2021 and 2024 at two neuro-ICUs at Charité-Universitätsmedizin Berlin. We prospectively studied patients with acute brain injury and poor neurologic prognosis defined by the absence of regaining decision-making capacity or sufficient autonomy. A total of 100 patients were included. None. Relatives were consulted to ascertain the patients' presumed wishes regarding the continuation or withdrawal of life-sustaining intensive care. The 10-item Santa Clara Strength of Religious Faith questionnaire was applied to measure the patient´s religiosity on a scale between 10 and 40 points. We applied the t-test for independent variables to evaluate the influence of religiosity on end-of-life decisions. To adjust for possible confounders like age, sex, nationality, and religion, we calculated a logistic regression as well as an analysis of variance calculation. In patients in whom intensive care was continued, the median score was significantly higher compared with patients in whom intensive care was withdrawn (28.1 ± 9.0 vs. 20.5 ± 8.3; p < 0.001; Cohens d = 0.875). This finding was reproduced in each denominational group. Religion, age, and sex showed no significant association with the end-of-life decision behavior. Germans chose withdrawal of therapy significantly more often than non-Germans (p = 0.01) but also showed significantly lower religiosity scores (21.9 vs. 27.9; p = 0.003). The RECONCILE study demonstrates that religiosity looks more important in influencing end-of-life decisions than religion. Higher levels of religiosity were associated with a preference for more aggressive treatment, even when neurologic prognosis is poor.

articles.title: Survival after neonatal chest compressions at birth: Temporal trends and prognostic factors in a population-based cohort, Queensland, Australia.
articles.abstract: To examine temporal trends and prognostic factors for 28-day survival among infants receiving chest compressions (CC) in Queensland, Australia. We conducted a retrospective population-based cohort study using the Queensland Perinatal Data Collection (2008-2024), including all liveborn CC recipients at birth. Temporal trends in crude 28-day survival were examined overall and by gestational age (GA) groups. Multivariable generalised estimating equations were used to identify factors independently associated with survival while accounting for clustering within birthing locations. Among 3,077 CC recipients, 70.5% established regular spontaneous breathing within 60 minutes of birth, and 89.0% survived to 28 days. Crude 28-day survival improved from 82% in 2008 to 89% in 2024 and was consistently higher in term (GA ≥37+0 weeks) than preterm infants. Compared with term infants, adjusted odds of survival declined with decreasing GA: 32+0 to 36+6 weeks (aOR 0.56, 95% CI 0.40-0.77), 28+0 to 31+6 weeks (aOR 0.35, 95% CI 0.23-0.54), and <28+0 weeks (aOR 0.17, 95% CI 0.12-0.23). However, after adjusting for cord pH or epinephrine administration, survival in infants born at 32+0 to 36+6 weeks did not differ significantly from term infants. Survival to 28 days among CC recipients was high and increased over time. Lower gestational age was the strongest independent prognostic factor for mortality, although the survival difference between term and moderate-to-late preterm infants was attenuated after adjustment for cord pH or epinephrine administration. Prospective studies assessing CC indications and measures of resuscitation quality are needed to optimise neonatal resuscitation and improve outcomes.

articles.title: Survival after out of hospital cardiac arrest in relation to AED usage in a multi response system including AED equipped drones.
articles.abstract: Early defibrillation is a key determinant of survival in out‑of‑hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA). In multi-response systems, it remains unclear which responders contribute most to early AED use and survival. This study compared first AED-attaching responders and their association with 30-day survival in a regional multi-response system. This registry‑based cohort study included OHCA cases in Västra Götaland Region, Sweden, between January 1, 2015, and December 31, 2024. Data were obtained from EMS, dispatch, and registry databases. The primary outcome was 30‑day survival. Among 9,413 OHCAs, EMS attached the first AED in 72% of cases, followed by on-duty first responders (ODFR) (18%), bystanders (6.0%), and community first responders (CFR) (4.5%). EMS attachment decreased from 77% to 67%, whereas CFR involvement increased from 1% to 13%. 30‑day survival was highest when AEDs were attached by bystanders (28%), compared with 9.0% for EMS, 8.7% for ODFR and 8.6% for CFR. Among witnessed OHCAs with an initial shockable rhythm, 30-day survival was highest in bystander-attached cases (62%), compared with 36% for CFR, 32% for ODFR, and 24% for EMS. In the multivariable analysis, bystander AED attachment was associated with higher odds of 30‑day survival compared with EMS (OR 2.25; 95% CI 1.77-2.85). In this multi-response system, survival was highest when AEDs were first attached by bystanders and remained higher after adjustment for known prognostic factors. This association likely reflects earlier access to defibrillation. These findings suggest that improving immediate access to defibrillation may have the greatest impact on OHCA outcomes.

articles.title: Early Prehospital Prediction of Neurological Outcome After Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest Derivation and External Validation of the MIRA-29 Score.
articles.abstract: Out-of-hospital cardiac (OHCA) arrest is a frequent emergency, and few patients will survive with good neurological outcome. Identification of patients with a low likelihood of meaningful recovery represents a major clinical challenge. Numerous scores have been developed to guide decision-making after OHCA, with variable goals and targets, but most of them have been validated on small cohorts, integrates variables not available in the prehospital field, or do have low prediction values. MIRA-29 score aimed to only rely on simple clinical variables, available in the prehospital setting. We hypothetized that such score will provide incremental neurological prognosis value at an early-stage following OHCA. MIRA-29 score was derived and internally validated over a five-year period on a prospective cohort of 1099 adult patients, including all OHCA treated by our territory dispatch center. Multivariate analysis identified independent variables within the database, that were used to optimize the prediction model using machine-learning and genetic algorithms. The score was subsequently validated externally on 82 696 patients extracted from the French national cardiac arrest registry (RéAC). Out from the 1099 patients, 85 patients (7.7%) had a favorable neurological outcome. Multivariate analysis identified five independent variables associated with neurological outcome: age, low-flow duration, number of external electric shock, epinephrine dose, and the OHCA site (street, public facility, home). After model optimization and machine-learning, age was not retained within the final model. External validation depicted a precision of 0.86 and a recall of 0.88 of the model. The F1-Score and accuracy are respectively 0.87 and 0.88, and specificity for a bad neurological prognosis is 0.99. MIRA‑29 strength lies on its ability to reliably identify patients with extremely high probability of poor neurological outcome, while being based on four simple clinical variables. The prospective validation of MIRA-29 in the clinical setting may evaluate its impact on clinical decision making.

articles.title: RescQTM: One-year implementation and feasibility results of a digitally enabled support pathway for bystanders of out-of-hospital cardiac arrest.
articles.abstract: Bystanders to out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) are at significant risk of psychological distress, yet no standardised support pathway exists for them in the UK. RescQ™ is a digital-first bystander support pathway embedded within regional prehospital and cardiac arrest care services. To evaluate the feasibility of embedding RescQ™ into routine emergency medical services (EMS) practice leading to appropriate contact with bystanders involved in OHCA. Secondary aims were to describe digital access, demand for liaison officer (LO) support, identification of younger bystanders, and EMS clinician acceptability. Prospective one-year regional service evaluation of RescQ™ across Essex, UK. Bystanders involved in eligible OHCA events were registered by EMS clinicians and provided with immediate access to secure digital resources. Bystanders could self-refer for additional support through LO. During the one-year evaluation, 220 of 432 eligible OHCA incidents had at least one bystander identified and the incident entered into the RescQ™ pathway, representing an incident-level capture rate of 50.9%. Across these incidents, 298 bystanders were identified, of whom 260 eligible adults were registered with RescQ™. Of registered adult bystanders, 96.2% accessed the digital resources at least once. Among all identified bystanders, 30/298 (10.1%) were aged under 18 years. Approximately 10% of registered bystanders self-referred for additional personalised LO support. Among 25 EMS clinician survey respondents who had used RescQTM in clinical practice, ratings indicated acceptability. RescQ™ demonstrated the feasibility of identifying and supporting bystanders following OHCA through a digitally enabled pathway, achieving incident-level capture above the pre-specified feasibility threshold and high website access among registered adults. These findings support further multi-region evaluation of implementation, sustainability and scalability across different EMS systems.

articles.title: Out-of-hospital cardiac arrests due to foreign body airway obstruction: A CanROC registry, retrospective cohort study.
articles.abstract: Foreign body airway obstruction (FBAO) is a treatable cause of out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA), but North American data are limited. Exploratory retrospective cohort study of EMS-treated OHCAs using the Canadian Resuscitation Outcomes Consortium (CanROC) registry (2005-2023), classified as obviously FBAO-related or of no obvious cause (presumed cardiac). Logistic regression compared Utstein characteristics between etiologies and identified factors associated with prehospital return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC) and survival to acute care discharge. Among 105,178 EMS-treated OHCAs, 1,106(1.1%) were obviously FBAO-related. Compared with cases of no obvious cause, obviously FBAO-related cases were older (median 73 vs 68 years, p<0.001), more often witnessed (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] 6.98[5.36-9.25]), more often attended by trained bystanders (aOR 3.30[2.41-4.41]), and less often had a shockable rhythm (aOR 0.11[0.07-0.15]). Obviously FBAO-related cases more often achieved prehospital ROSC (62.7% vs 37.8%; OR 2.77[2.44-3.13]), but survival did not differ (10.6% vs 9.0%,p=0.094). Within the obviously FBAO-related cohort, ROSC was associated with witnessed arrest (aOR 1.66[1.13-2.43]) and shorter EMS response time (aOR 0.95 per minute[0.92-0.99]). Survival was associated with younger age (aOR 0.76 per decade[0.61-0.93]), initial shockable rhythm (aOR 4.76[1.55-13.30]), and shorter EMS response time (aOR 0.81 per minute[0.66-0.98]). Survival was 18.1% and 0.8% among obviously FBAO-related OHCAs with and without prehospital ROSC, respectively. Obviously FBAO-related OHCAs are uncommon but clinically distinct. ROSC is frequent, yet survival remains low and is associated with early prehospital factors, supporting choking prevention initiatives, bystander training, and rapid EMS response.

articles.title: Commercially available multimodal LLMs for EEG-based prognostication after cardiac arrest.
articles.abstract: Machine-learning and deep-learning approaches have been successfully applied to EEG-based prognostication in comatose patients after cardiac arrest (CA), but typically rely on task-specific signal processing, feature extraction, and model development. Here, we investigated whether two commercially available multimodal large language models (LLMs) could predict neurological outcome directly from EEG images. Thirty-three comatose patients on the first day after CA from a prospective cohort were included. For each patient, a single 10-second EEG segment displayed using a longitudinal bipolar montage was rendered as PNG image. ChatGPT 5.4. and Claude Opus 4.7 were instructed to estimate the probability for favorable outcome for each case based on the EEG and a generic information block describing conditions of recordings. Five different prompting strategies were used, including few-shot prompting where four exemplary EEGs (not from the 33 patients) were provided. Predictive performance was quantified using AUC and accuracy. Across prompting strategies, the AUC ranged from 0.86 to 0.99 for ChatGPT and from 0.74 to 1.00 for Claude. The highest accuracy achieved by both models was 93.9% using few-shot prompting. As reference, a previously published dedicated deep-learning model achieved 100% on the same cohort. In this exploratory study of a small cohort, multimodal LLMs showed variable but potentially promising discrimination for predicting favorable outcome from single EEG image in comatose patients after CA. Performance depended substantially on prompt design. These findings require confirmation in a larger cohort.

articles.title: Community First Responder Activation Reduces the Negative Impact of AED Distance on Bystander Defibrillation After Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest.
articles.abstract: Early defibrillation is critical for survival after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA), yet bystander defibrillation remains uncommon despite the availability of automated external defibrillators (AEDs). We investigated whether HeartRunner community first responder activation increased the likelihood of bystander defibrillation and 30-day survival in relation to the distance to the nearest accessible AED. Linking data from the Danish Cardiac Arrest Registry, Danish AED Network, and HeartRunner application, we identified patients with OHCA eligible for HeartRunner activation during 2017-2021. Using street-network distances to the nearest accessible AED, we examined associations between HeartRunner activation, bystander defibrillation, and 30-day survival using multivariable logistic regression with interaction terms and targeted maximum likelihood estimation (TMLE). Among 5,753 OHCAs (median age, 74 years; 64% male; 78% in private locations), HeartRunner activation (41%) was associated with higher bystander defibrillation across AED distances (p-interaction = 0.004), with no interaction for 30-day survival (p-interaction = 0.054). Predicted bystander defibrillation with versus without HeartRunner activation was 9.6% vs 5.5% at Q1 (389 m), 10.0% vs 4.3% at median (717 m), and 13.0% vs 4.8% at Q3 (1,183 m). TMLE estimated a 6.1-percentage-point higher probability of bystander defibrillation (95% CI, 4.5-7.8; p<0.001) and a modest 1.8-percentage-point increase in 30-day survival (95% CI, 0.1-3.6; p=0.038) with HeartRunner activation. HeartRunner activation attenuated the decline in bystander defibrillation with increasing AED distance following OHCA, without a corresponding distance interaction for 30-day survival. Overall, TMLE supported higher bystander defibrillation and suggested a modest increase in 30-day survival with HeartRunner activation.

articles.title: Can the pulse oximeter tell us when the heart is back?
Ventilation feedback during resuscitation: lessons learned and implications for the future.
Follow-up of human papillomavirus positive patients after self-collection in the emergency department.
articles.journal: The American journal of emergency medicine
articles.abstract: Emergency department (ED) patients often lack sufficient primary care access and are disproportionately under-screened for cervical cancer compared with the general population. The recent FDA approval of self-collection for HPV testing at healthcare sites may facilitate cervical cancer screening for some patients. Thus, we investigated the proposition that the ED presents an opportunity to engage otherwise hard-to-reach individuals with cervical cancer screening via in-ED self-collection for HPV testing. While HPV negative individuals do not require further screening, HPV positive individuals require additional steps in the outpatient setting to complete screening. After recent completion of a feasibility study of HPV self-collection among eligible ED patients in which more than 80% of participants agreed to self-collect and approximately 75% successfully completed self-collection in the ED, we followed the individuals who tested positive for HPV to assess their rate of follow-up for outpatient completion of screening. We conducted follow-up at 150 days via electronic health record review and telephone survey to determine the follow-up rate for individuals who tested positive for HPV after in-ED self-collection. Among the individuals who successfully completed self-collection for HPV in the parent study, 24 (15.9%) tested positive for HPV. At 150 days, 7 (29.2%) out of 24 had completed screening (1 additional participant had scheduled upcoming screening). Individuals with higher triage acuity were less likely to follow up for additional screening. Additional supports are required to maximize follow-up for completion of screening among those who test positive after in-ED self-collection for HPV testing.

articles.title: Ultrasound-Guided Suprascapular Nerve Block Versus Intravenous Fentanyl for Analgesia in Patients Presenting to the Emergency Department With Traumatic Scapular Fractures.
articles.abstract: To compare the analgesic efficacy and safety of ultrasound-guided suprascapular nerve block with intravenous fentanyl in patients with traumatic scapular fractures. We conducted an open-label randomized controlled pilot trial in the emergency department (ED) of a Level I trauma center in North India. Adults with traumatic scapular fractures and Defense and Veterans Pain Rating Scale scores of 7 and higher, were randomly assigned to ultrasound-guided suprascapular nerve block or intravenous fentanyl (1 μg/kg). Pain scores were assessed at baseline and 30, 60, 120, 240, and 360 minutes. Secondary outcomes included rescue analgesia and adverse events. Sixty patients were randomly assigned to the 2 groups. Median baseline pain score was 10 in both groups. Pain scores were consistently lower with suprascapular nerve block, with median scores of 3 (interquartile [IQR] 2 to 5) versus 7 (IQR 6 to 8) at 30 minutes. Between-group differences were 4 (95% confidence interval [CI], 3 to 4) at 30 and 60 minutes, 2 (95% CI, 2 to 2) at 120 and 240 minutes, and 1 (95% CI, 1 to 2) at 360 minutes. Rescue analgesia was less frequent with suprascapular nerve block (13% versus 79%; risk difference, -66% [95% CI, 47.5 to 85.2]). Drowsiness was more common with fentanyl (12 versus 2 participants); hypotension occurred in 1 fentanyl recipient and paresthesia in 1 suprascapular nerve block recipient. In this pilot randomized trial, ultrasound-guided suprascapular nerve block provided greater and sustained pain relief, reduced rescue analgesia, and fewer systemic adverse effects than intravenous fentanyl in adults with traumatic scapular fractures. Larger multicenter trials are needed to confirm these findings and evaluate cumulative opioid use and longer-term outcomes.

articles.title: MPLA preconditioning protects against lethal radiation-combined burn injury with attenuation of KC/CXCL1-associated vascular leakage in mice.
articles.abstract: Radiation-combined burn injury (RCB), defined as concurrent irradiation and burn injury, is expected to be common in radiological or nuclear mass-casualty events and can be highly lethal. The mechanisms underlying the irradiation-burn interaction remain poorly understood, particularly whether it amplifies capillary leak and inflammatory mediator responses to drive early lethality. We examined whether repeated low-dose monophosphoryl lipid A (MPLA) preconditioning modulates this response and whether KC/CXCL1 contributes to vascular leakage. Male C57BL/6J mice underwent 6 Gy whole-body irradiation followed 1 h later by a 20% total body surface area full-thickness burn. MPLA (10 µg/mouse) or vehicle was administered intraperitoneally on days -4 and -3. We assessed 30-day survival, hemoconcentration, intravascular FITC-albumin retention, intestinal barrier endpoints, and cytokine/chemokine responses. A separate exploratory experiment evaluated pre-irradiation anti-KC/CXCL1 antibody treatment. Neither injury alone was lethal, whereas vehicle-treated RCB mice had 90% mortality (9 of 10 mice). Seven of these deaths occurred at 24-48 h after RCB. MPLA preconditioning increased 30-day survival from 10% to 80% (p = 0.0003) and eliminated deaths within 48 h. RCB induced hemoconcentration and tended to reduce FITC-albumin retention. Compared with vehicle-treated RCB mice, MPLA-preconditioned RCB mice had less hemoconcentration, significantly higher FITC-albumin retention, and lower mesenteric lymph node bacterial burden. MPLA preconditioning suppressed KC/CXCL1, which showed the largest absolute increase among measured cytokines/chemokines at 6 h. Anti-KC/CXCL1 antibody treatment significantly increased FITC-albumin retention at 6 h (p = 0.038). MPLA preconditioning improved survival after RCB. It may attenuate early inflammatory and vascular abnormalities. Exploratory antibody-treatment findings suggest a possible contribution of KC/CXCL1 to early vascular albumin leakage, warranting further validation.

articles.title: Earning a place in care by learning in it.
Does critical care training explain higher survival after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest?, Letter to the Editor.
Trends in United States Pediatric In-Hospital Cardiac Arrest Incidence and Mortality in a Nationally Representative Sample, 2009-2022.
articles.abstract: National estimates of pediatric in-hospital cardiac arrest (IHCA) incidence in the United States rely on a voluntary registry that may underrepresent smaller and critical access hospitals. Administrative datasets offer a nationally representative alternative. We estimated nationally representative pediatric IHCA incidence and mortality trends from 2009 through 2022. Serial cross-sectional analysis of five triennial editions of the Kids' Inpatient Database (2009-2022), identifying IHCA in children <18 years by ICD-9 (99.60, 99.63) and ICD-10 (5A12012) cardiopulmonary resuscitation procedure codes. Two hospitals with implausible CPR rates were excluded. Survey-weighted incidence per 1,000 hospitalizations and in-hospital mortality among resuscitated children were estimated overall and by neonatal status, complex chronic condition (CCC) status, ZIP-code income quartile, and US Census region. Trends were tested with survey-weighted quasi-Poisson regression across the full period and, as exploratory analyses, within the ICD-10 era (2016-2022). Observed IHCA incidence was 1.11/1,000 in 2009 and 1.22/1,000 in 2012, decreased to 1.11/1,000 at the ICD-10 transition and increased to 1.35/1,000 by 2022. IHCA incidence in children hospitalized with a CCC rose from 3.26 to 6.60/1,000 (6.2%/year, p<0.001), while incidence without CCC remained low. Incidence varied by socioeconomic status (lowest vs highest income quartile 1.78 vs 1.04/1,000 in 2022). In-hospital mortality ranged from 34.1% (2012) to 40.4% (2019), whereas IHCA deaths per 1,000 hospitalizations increased 1.7%/year (p<0.001), concentrated among children with a CCC. The incidence of pediatric IHCA increased among hospitalizations involving children with CCC and was higher among children who live in lower income areas. In-hospital mortality after CPR was largely stable, whereas arrest-related deaths per 1,000 hospitalizations increased among children with CCC. A single hospital's coding practices can materially distort national administrative estimates. What is already known Pediatric in-hospital cardiac arrest affects approximately 15,200 children annually in the United States, with this national estimate derived primarily from a voluntary registry that may underrepresent smaller and critical access hospitals. Administrative databases offer nationally representative coverage but rely on procedure codes that are susceptible to misclassification. What this study adds In this nationally representative administrative database sample spanning 2009-2022, this study demonstrated that: 1) the incidence of IHCA among children with complex chronic conditions (CCC) rose steadily and accounted for the substantial majority of events, 2) the overall IHCA incidence was higher among children who live in lower income areas with the gradient worsening over the period evaluated, and 3) in-hospital mortality after CPR increased only slightly (34-40%), whereas arrest-related deaths per 1,000 hospitalizations increased more, driven mainly by rising incidence among children with CCC, and 4) CPR coding at a single hospital can substantially distort national administrative estimates.

articles.title: Reply to: Does critical care training explain higher survival after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest?
Carboxypeptidase B1: A novel, targetable contributor to thromboembolic complications in severe acute pancreatitis?
articles.journal: The journal of trauma and acute care surgery
articles.abstract: Severe acute pancreatitis (SAP) is associated with increased thrombotic risk. Systemic release of pancreatic proteases in SAP may alter susceptibility to endogenous fibrinolysis, but this remains unexplored. Pancreatic carboxypeptidase B1 (CPB1) is a protease activated by trypsin that shares cleavage specificity with thrombin-activatable fibrinolysis inhibitor, which cleaves C-terminal lysine residues off fibrin, impairing co-localization of tissue plasminogen activator (tPA) and plasminogen and rendering clots resistant to fibrinolysis. We hypothesized that circulating CPB1 would be elevated in SAP patients and contribute to fibrinolytic resistance. Plasma and clinical data were prospectively collected from SAP patients (n=15), matched critically ill controls without pancreatitis (n=13), and healthy controls (n=4) with IRB approval and informed consent. CPB1 levels were measured through ELISA. Clot lysis assays assessed fibrinolysis in response to tPA. Healthy control plasma was tested with and without porcine pancreas CPB1 to assess the effect of CPB1 on fibrinolysis. Transition midpoints (TM's) were defined as the time to 50% clot lysis. Clinical data were analyzed using Mann-Whitney U and Fisher exact tests. Assay results were analyzed using Kruskall-Wallis test. Significance was set at P<0.05. Demographics were similar between groups. SAP patients had markedly elevated CPB1 levels (154.0 [58.4-388.0] ng/mL) compared with sick (7.0 [4.1-15.6] ng/mL, P<0.0001) and healthy controls (4.0 [2.1-4.4], P<0.001). Healthy control plasma supplemented with porcine pancreas CPB1 demonstrated complete disruption of fibrinolysis compared with healthy plasma without CPB1. SAP patients had the highest resistance to tPA-induced fibrinolysis, with significantly higher baseline TMs than critically ill controls (42.0 [21.7-126.6] vs. 22.8 [18.3-33.7], P=0.04). Patients with SAP have uniquely elevated circulating levels of CPB1, which may contribute to thromboembolism in SAP through fibrinolytic resistance. Further investigation into targeted CPB1 inhibition as a potential therapeutic strategy in SAP is warranted to potentially reduce development of organ failure and mortality. N/A (Basic Science).

articles.title: Pooled Prevalence of Infectious Diseases Among First Responders in the Prehospital Setting: A Systematic Review With Meta-Analysis by Occupation.
articles.abstract: First responders often work in unpredictable, uncontrolled environments, where exposure to infected patients and contaminated environments heighten the risk of communicable disease transmission. Their higher infection prevalence compared with the general population has driven the implementation of personal protective equipment, vaccination requirements, safety protocols, and infection prevention education. The aim of this systematic review and meta-analysis was to estimate the pooled prevalence of infections among first responders in the prehospital workers including paramedics, emergency medical technicians, patient transport staff, firefighters, police, and police officers. Embase, CINAHL, Web of Science, and PUBMED/Medline were systematically searched. Pooled prevalence estimates were calculated using random-effects models with restricted maximum likelihood estimation, with Freeman-Tukey double-arcsine transformation and back-transformation to the original prevalence scale. Heterogeneity was assessed using I2, τ2, and 95% prediction intervals. Meta-regression was used to examine potential sources of between-study heterogeneity, and small-study effects and potential publication bias were assessed using funnel plots and Egger's regression test. Risk of bias was investigated using the AXIS tool. Following the initial search, 34,874 articles were identified, of which 88 were full-text screened. Of these, 22 studies representing 19,188 first responders were included in this systematic review. The pooled prevalences of hepatitis B and C were 6.2% (95% CI 4.5%-8.2%) and 1.8% (95% CI 0.9%-2.9%), respectively. Around 4% (95% CI 2.6%-5.9%) of the first responders had MRSA colonization. Current or past infection with COVID-19 among non-vaccinated first responders was 13.6% (95% CI 4.8%-25.9%), which reduced to 7.3% (95% CI 3.6%-12%) after exclusion of studies with high risk of bias. Of the known study characteristics, geographic region significantly contributed to heterogeneity, explaining 36.7% of between-study variance, p = 0.039. Infectious disease prevalence varied across pathogens, occupations, and geographical settings among first responders. These findings should be interpreted in light of substantial heterogeneity and limitations in the available evidence but may help inform infection prevention, occupational health policy, vaccination strategies, and future research in first responder services.

articles.title: Microbiota-gut-brain axis dysregulation in irritable bowel syndrome: mechanisms, clinical evidence, and therapeutic implications. a narrative review.
articles.abstract: Irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) is a heterogeneous disorder of gut-brain interaction in which altered visceral sensitivity, motility, immune activity, epithelial permeability, and microbial metabolism may interact. Microbiota-related associations are frequently reported, but their direction and causal relevance remain uncertain. This narrative review critically examines clinical and mechanistic evidence concerning microbiota-gut-brain communication in IBS, including short-chain fatty acids, bile acids, gaseous metabolites, tryptophan metabolism, environmental exposures, and microbiota-directed interventions. The literature was selected for relevance and interpretability rather than through a systematic evidence-synthesis protocol. Across studies, microbiota-associated differences vary by phenotype, diet, geography, sampling site, and analytical method; no validated IBS-specific microbial signature has emerged. Bile acid metabolism, mucosal immune-neural interactions, and microbial metabolites provide plausible mechanistic links, although much evidence remains associative. Low-FODMAP dietary treatment and rifaximin in appropriately selected patients have clinical trial support, whereas probiotic effects are formulation dependent and fecal microbiota transplantation remains investigational. Microbiome-based precision treatment requires longitudinal phenotyping, standardized sampling, functional multi-omics, and intervention studies demonstrating that microbial or metabolic changes mediate clinical benefit. Microbiome profiling is not yet established as a routine diagnostic test for IBS.

articles.title: [Emergency critical care in the emergency department].
articles.abstract: Emergency critical care (ECC) provides early, ongoing critical care outside the intensive care unit (ICU). This narrative review describes organizational models and evidence in emergency medicine. Predominantly retrospective, single-center studies indicate that critical care is initiated earlier and that there are fewer subsequent inpatient ICU admissions. Neither a consistent mortality benefit nor the superiority of any model has been established. ECC supports early care, coordination of complex care pathways, and needs-based resource allocation, guided by the principle: the right patient in the right care setting.

articles.title: Research on the morphology and injury mechanism of pilon fractures.
articles.journal: European journal of trauma and emergency surgery : official publication of the European Trauma Society
articles.abstract: Understanding the relationship between injury mechanisms and fracture morphology in high-energy Pilon fractures is essential for optimizing preoperative planning and surgical outcomes. To investigate the associations between injury mechanisms and fracture morphology in high-energy Pilon fractures and to provide a theoretical basis for precision diagnosis and treatment. This retrospective study included 192 patients with high-energy Pilon fractures treated at Lianyungang Second People's Hospital between January 2010 and December 2024. Using a standardized "trauma history-first plus imaging cross-validation" protocol, patients were categorized into 5 groups: dorsiflexion, varus, valgus, plantarflexion, and neutral. Two senior orthopedic surgeons (≥ 10 years of experience) independently and blindly assessed anteroposterior and lateral tibiofibular radiographs, CT scans, and three-dimensional reconstructions. Evaluated parameters included fibular fracture level and type, tibial fragment distribution, fracture angle, and Topliss classification. Interobserver reliability was assessed using Cohen's kappa coefficient. Group comparisons were performed using the chi-square (χ²) test or Fisher's exact test with Bonferroni correction for multiple comparisons. Statistical significance was defined as P < 0.05. Among the 192 patients, 154 (80.2%) were male and 38 (19.8%) were female. The mean (SD) age was 43.38 (12.56) years (range, 14-71 years). Interobserver agreement was substantial for injury mechanism classification (κ = 0.82; 95% CI, 0.75-0.89) and core morphological assessments (κ = 0.87; 95% CI, 0.81-0.93). Fracture morphology differed significantly among mechanism groups (P < 0.05). Dorsiflexion injuries were characterized by the "medial + anterolateral + Die-punch" fragment pattern (45.0%; 95% CI, 23.1%-66.9%), fracture angles > 90° (65.0%), and coronal Y-shaped fractures (25.0%). Varus injuries predominantly showed the "anterolateral + posterolateral + medial + Die-punch" pattern (32.5%) and simple sagittal split fractures (40.0%). Valgus injuries were associated with comminuted fibular fractures (64.3%) and coronal V/Y-shaped tibial fractures (35.7%). Plantarflexion injuries typically involved posterolateral fragments (61.5%) and fracture angles > 90° (80.8%). Neutral injuries were characterized by complex multifragmentary comminuted fractures with Die-punch collapse (33.7%). There is a significant and reproducible association between injury mechanisms and fracture morphology in high-energy Pilon fractures. This mechanism-based morphological characterization may provide an objective reference for preoperative assessment and individualized surgical planning. The clinical utility and prognostic value of this classification framework still need to be verified in further prospective studies with clinical outcome endpoints.
