Risk factors of in-hospital mortality in adult emergency department patients with atraumatic acute abdominal pain: a retrospective cohort study.
articles.abstract: Acute abdominal pain (AAP) accounts for 7-10% of adult emergency department (ED) visits and represents a heterogeneous presentation. While diagnostic pathways have improved, early prognostic assessment remains limited. Identifying routinely available parameters associated with in-hospital mortality may provide prognostic information at initial triage. Therefore, we aimed to identify such parameters in adult AAP patients. We conducted a retrospective cohort study of adult patients assigned to the "abdominal pain in adults" Manchester Triage System flowchart at the University Hospital Bonn ED (2023-2025). Candidate predictors comprised all structured parameters available at initial triage. Missing data were handled using multiple imputation. Group differences were assessed using Fisher's exact and Mann-Whitney U tests. We fitted a multivariable logistic regression model to assess associations between candidate predictors and in-hospital mortality. P-values were Bonferroni-adjusted. A focused literature search contextualized mortality. Among 6,370 encounters, 94 (1.5%) ended in death during the ED encounter or subsequent hospitalization. In-hospital mortality (1.5%) was within previously published ranges (0.4-8.0%). Patients who died were older and had lower systolic and diastolic blood pressure and SpO₂, higher pain NRS scores, and a different distribution of GCS scores at initial triage after adjustment for multiple testing. In multivariable analysis, age (OR 1.067 per year; 95% CI 1.052-1.082), lower diastolic blood pressure (OR 0.953 per mmHg; 95% CI 0.932-0.976), higher heart rate (OR 1.022 per beat/min; 95% CI 1.009-1.036), lower SpO₂ (OR 0.885 per percentage point; 95% CI 0.833-0.940), and higher pain NRS scores (OR 1.283 per point; 95% CI 1.126-1.462) were associated with mortality after adjustment for multiple testing. Among patients who died, vascular or bleeding disorders, bowel ischemia, and malignancy were the leading diagnostic categories. In adult ED patients presenting with atraumatic AAP, in-hospital mortality was 1.5%, within the previously reported range. Age, lower diastolic blood pressure, higher heart rate, lower SpO₂, and higher pain intensity were independently associated with mortality after adjustment for multiple testing. These routinely available parameters may provide prognostic information at initial triage, but their value for improving risk prediction or clinical decision-making requires further investigation.

articles.title: Field Amputation by helicopter emergency service personnel: A cross-sectional survey of clinical practice and experience within air ambulance services in England.
articles.abstract: Field Amputation (FA) is a rare, but potentially life-saving procedure undertaken by helicopter emergency medical services (HEMS) in the UK. Literature pertaining to FA predominantly originates from outside the UK, where the operational, clinical and legal differences make its applicability to the UK uncertain. Consequently, the severe lack of FA reports from the UK mean that FA is poorly documented in this setting. The aim is to establish the current prehospital FA clinical guidance and practice in the UK. An electronic, cross-sectional survey was sent to all UK HEMS. The survey sought to improve understanding of clinical practice, including service provision, scope of practice, equipment, training, governance and incidences of FA. Surveys were analysed with descriptive statistics and descriptive thematic analysis. 15 HEMS responded, with 14 included for final analysis after one response was excluded. All respondents were from England. Every HEMS (n = 14, 100%) could provide FA, with 12 (86%) having a Clinical Practice Guideline specific to FA. Four services (29%) had undertaken FA within the last five years, totalling six cases, which were deemed notable given the absence of case reports from the UK in that time. A Gigli saw was the most popular instrument for bone disarticulation (n = 13, 93%). Unlike the USA and Korea, no respondents used hospital response teams to provide FA. FA service provision is widely available across England, with cases of FA being undertaken, yet little standardisation nationally. A national or international registry of every FA case could provide further insights into this area of clinical practice.

articles.title: A Peer-Supported Guide for Firefighters Healing from Burn Injury: Bridging Survivor Experience and Clinical Expertise.
articles.journal: Journal of burn care & research : official publication of the American Burn Association
articles.abstract: Firefighters remain at risk for burn and inhalation injuries despite advances in protective equipment and operational safety. Recovery and return to duty are shaped by physical demands, emotional challenges, occupational culture, and financial pressures. Existing resources address important aspects of burn recovery but are fragmented across multiple sources, leaving firefighters without a single, structured guide spanning the continuum of recovery. A descriptive, collaborative approach was used to develop a firefighter-specific recovery guide. Participants included a firefighter who sustained a line-of-duty burn injury, members of the fire department peer support team, fire service leadership, and multidisciplinary burn center clinicians. The firefighter burn survivor's reflective journaling of recovery served as the catalyst for the project. Through monthly meetings, participants examined the burn recovery continuum from fireground injury through rehabilitation and return to duty, identifying educational gaps and collaboratively developing the guide's content. The primary outcome was the development of The Burn Recovery Red Book: A Peer-Supported Guide for Firefighters Healing from a Burn Injury, a firefighter-specific resource integrating lived experience, peer support perspectives, and clinician-developed patient education. It provides structured guidance across the continuum of burn recovery spanning on-scene response, inpatient burn center care, discharge planning, home recovery, rehabilitation, and return-to-duty. The collaborative development of The Burn Recovery Red Book: A Peer-Supported Guide for Firefighters Healing from a Burn Injury produced a firefighter-specific guide that addresses the need for a single, structured reference to support recovery from injury through return to duty. This approach may be adaptable for other burn centers and fire departments seeking to strengthen recovery education and return-to-duty preparation.

articles.title: Association Between Weight Percentile and Non-Accidental Trauma in Pediatric Burn Patients Aged 0-4 Years: A Retrospective Cohort Study.
articles.journal: Journal of burn care & research : official publication of the American Burn Association
articles.abstract: Early recognition of non-accidental trauma (NAT) in pediatric burn patients remains challenging because no single clinical feature reliably distinguishes abusive from accidental injuries. Although poor growth has been associated with maltreatment, its relationship with NAT in pediatric burn patients is unclear. This study evaluated whether weight percentile is associated with NAT. A retrospective cohort study was conducted using the burn registry of a single burn center. Children aged 0-4 years admitted with burn injuries between 2010 and 2021 were included if NAT status and admission weight percentile were available. Multivariable logistic regression evaluated the association between weight percentile and NAT after adjustment for age, sex, race, and total body surface area (TBSA) burned. Sensitivity analyses examined weight percentile thresholds (<5th, <10th, and <25th percentile). Among 830 patients, 69 (8.3%) had documented NAT. Children with NAT had lower median weight percentiles (46.6 vs. 64.5; p<0.001) and larger burns (median TBSA, 5.0% vs. 3.0%; p<0.001). After adjustment, each 10-percentile decrease in weight percentile was associated with increased odds of NAT (adjusted odds ratio [aOR], 1.16; 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.06-1.26; p<0.001). Weight percentile <10th (aOR, 4.10; 95% CI, 1.93-8.69; p<0.001) and <25th percentile (aOR, 2.09; 95% CI, 1.17-3.75; p=0.013) were also independently associated with NAT. Model discrimination was modest (AUC=0.674). Lower weight percentile was independently associated with NAT in pediatric burn patients aged 0-4 years. Although insufficient as a standalone screening tool, weight percentile is an objective, readily available clinical characteristic that may complement evaluation of suspected maltreatment.

articles.title: Skin Graft Thickness Consistency: A Comparison of Traditional Dermatome and Rotating Circular Blade Technology.
articles.journal: Journal of burn care & research : official publication of the American Burn Association
articles.abstract: Our objective was to evaluate the accuracy and intra-graft consistency of split-thickness skin graft thickness using a traditional dermatome versus a dermatome with a rotating circular blade. A controlled cadaveric study was conducted with operators across four experience levels. Each participant harvested split-thickness skin grafts using both devices set to 0.009 inches (0.229 mm). Grafts were obtained from adjacent locations on the back and leg. Three 6-mm punch biopsies per graft were analyzed histologically for thickness. Outcomes included deviation from the depth setting and intra-graft variability. Statistical comparisons included independent t-tests and analysis of variance. A total of 118 samples were analyzed. Traditional dermatome grafts were significantly thicker than intended (mean 0.0119 inches (0.30 mm); +33%), whereas grafts taken with the rotating circular blade dermatome were closer to target (mean 0.0080 inches [0.20 mm]; -11%) (p = 0.046). Intra-graft variability was significantly lower with the rotating circular blade dermatome (F(1,118) = 26.75, p < 0.001). No significant differences were observed by operator experience or donor site. The rotating circular blade dermatome demonstrated superior depth accuracy and reduced intra-graft variability compared with traditional dermatome. These findings suggest that device design may mitigate operator-dependent variability and improve reproducibility in split-thickness skin graft harvesting.

articles.title: Predictors of in-hospital mortality, sepsis and prolonged length of stay in burn patients: a ten-year monocentric experience and comparison with the Baux and revised Baux scores.
articles.journal: Journal of burn care & research : official publication of the American Burn Association
articles.abstract: Burn mortality is usually predicted with the Baux and revised Baux scores, which do not include comorbidity; the independent role of psychiatric disease is also poorly defined. We reviewed 793 consecutive burn patients (630 adults, 163 children) admitted to a regional referral centre between 2016 and 2025. In adults, logistic models for in-hospital mortality, sepsis, and prolonged length of stay (at least 30 days) used age group, burn size by total body surface area, inhalation injury, and the Charlson Comorbidity Index as covariates, with internal bootstrap validation. Adult in-hospital mortality was 7.8% (49 of 630); no child died. Independent predictors of mortality were age 85 years or older (odds ratio 18.9), burn size 40% or more (odds ratio 40.6), inhalation injury (odds ratio 4.29), and a comorbidity index of 2 or more (odds ratio 14.2). Psychiatric disorders, not captured by the comorbidity index, were also independently associated with mortality (odds ratio 2.83). The multivariable model, a Baux-based model, and a revised Baux-based model (both including the comorbidity index) had almost identical discrimination (optimism-corrected 0.941, 0.955, 0.957; pairwise p>0.05). For sepsis and prolonged stay, burn size and age dominated, while comorbidity lost significance; the crude association between sepsis and mortality disappeared after adjustment, whereas sepsis remained strongly associated with prolonged stay (adjusted odds ratio 10.8). A multivariable model discriminates as well as the Baux scores while allowing comorbidity and psychiatric history to be quantified.

articles.title: Emergency medical service capacity and prehospital stroke care in Africa: a critical narrative review.
articles.abstract: Stroke is a time-critical medical emergency in which rapid recognition, transport, and treatment are essential to preserving neurological function. Yet across much of Africa, the prehospital systems required to support timely stroke care remain fragmented, underdeveloped, or entirely absent. This critical narrative review examines the evidence on emergency medical service (EMS) capacity for acute stroke care in Africa. Available evidence demonstrates major deficiencies across the entire prehospital stroke pathway. Formal EMS systems are absent in many African countries, and where services exist, ambulance coverage is limited, unevenly distributed, and concentrated largely in urban settings. Community awareness of stroke symptoms and emergency response pathways remains critically low, while reliance on self-transport, pharmacies, traditional healers, and informal care pathways contributes to substantial delays in hospital presentation. Across multiple African settings, most patients with stroke arrive at healthcare facilities hours or days after symptom onset, well beyond established therapeutic windows for reperfusion therapy. The review argues that these delays are not isolated failures of individual behavior but manifestations of broader structural deficiencies in emergency care systems, transport infrastructure, health financing, and stroke preparedness. Limited integration of stroke into national EMS planning, inadequate investment in emergency care infrastructure, and the absence of African-specific implementation research have collectively constrained the development of effective prehospital stroke systems across the continent. Improving stroke outcomes in Africa will require coordinated investment in EMS infrastructure, culturally appropriate stroke awareness programs, community health worker training, mobile health-supported emergency coordination, and integrated prehospital-to-hospital stroke pathways. This evidence is drawn from Ghana, Nigeria, and South Africa, the minority of African countries with published, country-level EMS and stroke-pathway data. Findings and recommendations should be interpreted as characterizing this documented subset rather than the continent as a whole.

articles.title: Competences of Paramedics in Prehospital Emergency Care: An Umbrella Review.
articles.abstract: The aim of this umbrella review is to describe and define the competences required of paramedics in out-of-hospital emergency medical care. The review was conducted in accordance with the methodological guidelines of the Joanna Briggs Institute. Keywords were defined according to the PCC-based inclusion and exclusion criteria. Data were retrieved from the Medic, PubMed, Scopus, CINAHL and ProQuest databases. Publications in Finnish and English were included. The search was conducted in 2024. Five reviewers independently screened the eligibility of reviews based on titles and abstracts (n = 2224) and full texts (n = 105). In the final stage, 20 studies were selected and critically appraised. Methodological quality was assessed using the JBI critical appraisal checklist. Data were analysed using inductive content analysis. Confidence in the synthesised findings was assessed using the GRADE-CERQual approach. Eight reviews were included in the final synthesis. The competences required in out-of-hospital emergency medical care were categorised into five main domains: interpersonal and teamwork competence; cognitive and decision-making competence; professionalism and ethical competence; clinical competence; and competence across paramedic certification levels and in special or high-stress situations. This umbrella review provides a comprehensive synthesis of the competences required of paramedics in out-of-hospital emergency medical care, both currently and in the future. Furthermore, future research should examine which educational and assessment approaches most effectively support the ongoing maintenance and development of competence within a changing operational context and an expanding scope of practice.

Uncommon presentation of median arcuate ligament syndrome in a young male treated with simultaneous robot-assisted release and cholecystectomy: a case report.
articles.abstract: Median arcuate ligament syndrome (MALS), also known as celiac artery compression syndrome, is a rare vascular and neurogenic disorder caused by external compression of the celiac artery and surrounding neural structures by the median arcuate ligament. It typically presents with postprandial abdominal pain, nausea, and weight loss and is most commonly reported in females between the third and fifth decades of life. We present an unusual case of a 20-year-old male with persistent postprandial abdominal pain for years who lost 20 pounds over the past year. He was found to have peak systolic velocities consistent with greater than 70% hemodynamically significant celiac artery stenosis on mesenteric duplex ultrasound, indicative of vascular compression. Additional imaging demonstrated no significant biliary obstruction but identified gallbladder sludge, contributing to diagnostic complexity due to overlapping symptom profiles. The patient underwent simultaneous robot-assisted median arcuate ligament release with celiac plexus neurolysis and robot-assisted cholecystectomy. The procedure was completed without complications, with minimal blood loss, and the patient was discharged in stable condition on postoperative day one. In the weeks following discharge, the patient developed postoperative gastritis with episodic severe abdominal pain, with full symptomatic resolution confirmed at approximately one year postoperatively. This case highlights an atypical demographic presentation of MALS and demonstrates the feasibility and safety of performing concurrent robotic procedures to address coexisting abdominal pathology in a single operative session. Increased awareness of atypical presentations may reduce diagnostic delay, while robotic-assisted approaches may offer a precise and effective minimally invasive treatment strategy for carefully selected patients.

articles.title: A rare case of Valentino syndrome presenting as acute right lower quadrant pain: a case report.
articles.abstract: Valentino syndrome is a rare clinical entity in which a perforated peptic ulcer causes extravasation of gastrointestinal contents into the right lower quadrant, mimicking acute appendicitis. It is seldom reported in the literature but has significant diagnostic implications due to its deceptive presentation. A 33-year-old male presented with a 4-day history of worsening right lower quadrant abdominal pain accompanied by nausea. There was a long history of intermittent NSAID use. On physical examination, the right lower quadrant was tender with guarding and rebound tenderness. Laboratory tests showed leukocytosis. Computed tomography demonstrated an 8-mm appendix suspicious for early acute appendicitis, together with mild prepyloric antral wall thickening and surrounding perigastric inflammatory changes, raising suspicion of a contained peptic ulcer perforation. Diagnostic laparoscopy was initially performed and was converted to open surgery after identification of the suspected gastric perforation. Intraoperatively, the appendix was mildly inflamed and hyperemic, and an appendectomy was performed. Further exploration revealed fibrinopurulent inflammatory changes over the anterior gastric region, with the suspected perforation contained by the omentum. No active leakage was observed, and the suspected perforation site was reinforced with omentopexy. The postoperative course was uneventful; the patient was discharged on postoperative day 5 with dietary, PPI and NSAID avoidance counseling. Valentino syndrome should be included in the differential diagnosis of right lower quadrant pain, especially in patients with risk factors for peptic ulcer disease. Early imaging and thorough evaluation can prevent misdiagnosis and reduce morbidity.

Securing Cell-Free Expression: Safeguards for Distributed Biomanufacturing.
articles.abstract: Cell-free expression (CFE) is an acellular biomanufacturing platform capable of producing diverse biomolecules, including proteins, enzymes, and mRNA, outside of living cells. Unlike traditional bioproduction, which requires sterile culture systems and large-scale bioreactors, CFE enables rapid, modular, and decentralized synthesis. CFE extracts can be freeze-dried, stored for extended periods, and reactivated on demand by simply adding a nucleic acid template. This makes it particularly suited for point-of-need applications such as diagnostics, vaccines, and potentially therapeutics in remote, resource-limited, or emergency settings. However, the same features introduce novel biosecurity concerns. Commercially available CFE kits already support the production of bacteriophages and virus-like particles with minimal specialized equipment. As benchtop DNA synthesis and CFE technologies become increasingly accessible, barriers of skill, facilities, and resources are significantly reduced, enabling malicious actors or small autonomous groups to generate harmful biological agents. To address these risks while enabling safe deployment, we recommend: (1) investing in yield optimization and the development of modular, good manufacturing practice-compatible CFE units for distributed manufacturing (performance and scalability); (2) engineering CFE systems with bioorthogonal or otherwise nontransferable components to reduce potential misuse (intrinsic safety feature); and (3) implementing risk-based restrictions for different CFE formulations, balancing innovation with security oversight (tiered access controls). By combining these measures, CFE can be responsibly integrated into global health security infrastructure, delivering its transformative benefits without compromising biosecurity.

Crevasse Fall-Related Trauma Referred to a Swiss Level I Trauma Centre: A Retrospective Descriptive Case Series (2013-2023).
articles.abstract: Falls into glacier crevasses represent an uncommon but potentially life-threatening mechanism of injury, with clinical presentations ranging from minor injuries to severe multisystem trauma. This study aimed to characterize the clinical presentation, injury patterns, physiological disturbances, management pathways, and in-hospital outcomes of patients with crevasse fall-related trauma referred to a Swiss Level I trauma centre. We conducted a retrospective descriptive case series including patients aged ≥16 years with traumatic injuries related to crevasse falls who were referred between 2013 and 2023. Cases were identified through electronic medical record screening and manual verification. Demographic data, accident characteristics, injury severity scores (NACA, AIS, ISS), physiological and laboratory findings, therapeutic management, and in-hospital outcomes were extracted. Results are presented using descriptive statistics. Twenty-eight patients were included (mean age 41.2 years; 23/28 [82.1%] male), of whom 21/28 (75.0%) were non-Swiss nationals. Crevasse falls occurred most frequently during ski touring (12/27 [44.4%]) and high-altitude mountaineering (11/27 [40.7%]), with seasonal peaks in spring and late summer. The median estimated fall depth was 20 m (IQR 10-25 m). Injury patterns were heterogeneous and frequently multisystemic; fractures occurred in 23/28 patients (82.1%), often involving multiple anatomical regions. An ISS ≥16 was observed in 16/28 patients (57.1%), all of whom fulfilled the study definition of polytrauma. Hypothermia was documented in 14/28 patients (50.0%), ICU admission was required in 11/28 patients (39.3%), and surgical intervention was performed in 20/28 patients (71.4%). In-hospital mortality was 2/28 (7.1%). In this referral-based cohort, crevasse fall-related trauma showed heterogeneous injury severity, with frequent multisystem injuries, physiological disturbances, and substantial requirements for surgical and intensive care management.
